introduction: Real-world robot policies must do more than reproduce demonstrated trajectories: they must interpret high-level task instructions, reason about the current environment, and continually adapt their plans and actions as new observations arrive. This requirement has motivated the use of large-scale pretrained models as policy backbones, from vision–language–action models (VLAs) that inherit semantic knowledge from vision–language models (VLMs) to world action models (WAMs) that exploit the spatiotemporal and physical priors of video generative models. However, existing VLAs and WAMs still struggle with zero-shot generalization and in-context learning, partly due to the scarcity of real-world robot data and catastrophic forgetting during robot-specific adaptation, which undermine pretrained capabilities.

Against this backdrop, recent GPT-6-Astra has demonstrated promising embodied capabilities, surpassing several VLAs/WAMs policies in RoboDojo evaluations and raising the prospect of translating general-purpose multimodal reasoning more directly into physical action. However, encouraging results in controlled tabletop settings do not yet establish whether these capabilities extend to functionally diverse environments, realistic task objectives, and sustained compositions of heterogeneous skills. To investigate this question, we adopt EBench, a diagnostic simulation benchmark comprising 26 tasks across nine scene categories, spanning household, retail, and industrial environments and jointly covering mobile manipulation, long-horizon multistage execution, and dexterous, high-precision interaction.

Beyond capturing the complexity of real-world tasks, EBench introduces controlled distribution shifts in backgrounds, objects, instructions, and their combinations. To further investigate capability differences between VLAs/WAMs and agents-based policy, we additionally introduce a compositional task: the training set contains the constituent single tasks performed in the same scene, whereas evaluation requires composing two tasks into a single task sequence. This combination of realistic task settings, controlled distribution shifts, and compositional evaluation provides a testbed for examining whether Astra can translate task understanding and in-context demonstrations into reliable completion of complex, multi-stage tasks through closed-loop interaction, and how its strengths and limitations compare with those of specialized VLAs and WAMs.
benchmark: EBench is a diagnostic simulation benchmark for generalist robot manipulation. It spans nine scene categories covering household, retail, industrial, and logistics settings, and includes mobile manipulation, multistage activities, and dexterous tabletop interaction. Tasks are annotated by scene, constituent skills, temporal horizon, precision, and mobility. The benchmark also defines evaluation conditions with controlled changes to backgrounds, objects, instructions, and their combinations.

We choose EBench to examine whether Astra can translate general-purpose multimodal reasoning into reliable execution of tasks with concrete everyday and work-related objectives. Its simulated environments place objects and actions within functional contexts, including food preparation, household cleaning, retail checkout, and component assembly. Successful execution requires the agent to relate object functions and spatial relationships to the task objective and coordinate the operations needed to achieve it. For example, sandwich preparation and retail checkout involve multiple object interactions whose order and outcomes determine subsequent actions. Mobile manipulation further requires coordinating robot repositioning with object handling as the spatial configuration changes. These settings allow us to investigate whether Astra can use task instructions and demonstrations to organize a complete procedure, track progress, and adapt its actions to the evolving environment. EBench’s task annotations further support analysis of how this execution capability varies across operating modes, task horizons, and precision requirements.

Evaluation scope. Our main evaluation uses the EBench test_mini split and covers 26 task types: 19 mobile-manipulation tasks and seven tabletop-manipulation tasks. The retained evaluation set contains 510 episodes with archived server-terminal scores, comprising 20 instances for each of 24 tasks and 15 instances each for make_sandwich and microwave. All 510 episodes in the main evaluation use a fixed task-specific historical demonstration package for in-context learning (ICL). Each task–instance pair contributes one retained terminal result. The reported benchmark aggregates refer to this retained test_mini evaluation set.

Performance is evaluated using success rate (SR) and Score. For each task, SR denotes the proportion of evaluated instances satisfying the server-side success criterion, whereas Score is the mean normalized terminal score, reflecting partial completion under task-specific scoring rules. Overall SR and Score are computed as unweighted averages of the corresponding task-level metrics across all 26 tasks. Comparisons between the agent-based policy and representative VLA and WAM policies on EBench, including the evaluated systems and results, are presented in the subsequent experiments section.
integration: We evaluate GPT-6-Astra with reasoning effort set to high. Each episode begins with a fresh model thread, and subsequent decisions use the interaction history accumulated within that episode. Recovery may reconstruct a thread from confirmed execution history and current observations, while interaction history is not explicitly transferred between evaluation episodes. The model receives three RGB views—overview, left_wrist, and right_wrist—together with both end-effector poses, gripper state, planar-base pose, and the current simulator timestep. All three views are provided initially; subsequent tool calls return the camera subset requested by the model. Live observations do not include depth, ground-truth object poses, camera calibration, or segmentation. Joint states support internal execution and logging but are not directly supplied to the model. To maintain consistent environment-level evaluation conditions, Astra is subject to the same task-specific physics-step limits and camera-access restrictions as the compared policies. Live camera access is restricted to overview, left_wrist, and right_wrist, with no access to a head-camera view. Intermediate evaluator states, task scores, and subgoal-completion signals are withheld during normal policy execution. Final evaluation feedback is returned only when the episode terminates through task completion or exhaustion of the server-side physics-step budget.

All 510 episodes use in-context demonstrations. We prepare one fixed historical demonstration package per task and reuse it across that task’s evaluation instances. Reference trajectories are selected offline, visually inspected, and annotated by operational phase. Each package contains 10–18 keyframe images, descriptions of the operation sequence and arm roles, and selected numerical examples of measured robot states and recorded action targets. At the beginning of each episode, the demonstration text, numerical excerpts, and labeled images are inserted after the shared task prompt and before the current observation. Explicit boundary markers distinguish historical reference material from the current episode. The model is instructed to adapt the demonstrated procedure and relative geometry using live observations, without automatic replay of recorded coordinates. Demonstrations are reintroduced when recovery reconstructs the model context. The reference trajectories do not carry official success labels, and their scene overlap with the evaluation instances has not been verified.

Apart from the task instruction, the initial user-prompt template is shared across tasks. It explicitly instructs the model to close the gripper while stationary, allow stabilization, perform a 0.01 m test lift over at least 16 interpolation steps, and hold for 8–16 physics steps while checking whether the object follows the gripper. Orientation and base pose are to remain fixed during this check. This grasp-verification procedure is supplied guidance. Additional task-context files, pre-executed gripper calibration, and historical action-prefix replay are disabled.

Astra controls the ARX Lift 2 dual-arm mobile robot through a fixed end-effector control interface. Given visual observations and robot state, the model specifies end-effector poses, gripper commands, base targets, and action durations. The execution layer translates these requests into simulator commands; no learned VLA or WAM policy generates or refines the actions. Only robot-interaction tools are available to the model. Actions execute in chunks, after which the model receives updated RGB images and measured robot state to inform its next decision.

Execution is bounded by EBench’s task-specific simulation horizons, without additional aggregate token, tool-call, or wall-clock limits on the policy phase. Task success and partial credit are determined by the EBench server. If the model stops issuing actions before a terminal result is available, the runner holds the robot configuration and continues advancing the simulation to obtain the terminal evaluation. Reported outcomes include this automatic holding phase.
settings: We consider two evaluation settings: seen tasks and unseen task compositions. In the seen-task setting, the evaluated task types are represented in the training data of the VLA and WAM policies, while Astra receives one fixed demonstration package per task through in-context learning (ICL). Each package is curated from a single historical trajectory and contains selected keyframe images, phase-based descriptions, and excerpts of measured robot states and recorded action targets. These materials describe arm and base roles, interaction order, relative object geometry, and observable completion checkpoints. The package is provided at the beginning of each episode and reused across evaluation instances of the same task; Astra adapts the demonstrated procedure using the current instruction and live observations. The 26-task, 510-episode test_mini evaluation described above constitutes our seen-task evaluation.

In the unseen-composition setting, the VLA and WAM policies are trained on the constituent tasks performed individually in the same scene, but not on the target two-task sequence. Evaluation requires completing the two tasks as a single ordered procedure. Astra is evaluated zero-shot in this setting, receiving the composed task instruction and live observations without in-context demonstrations of either the constituent tasks or their composition. Both settings incorporate environmental and instructional variation under the EBench protocol. The terms seen and unseen refer to whether the evaluated task types or compositions are represented in the VLA/WAM benchmark training data; they do not imply unchanged evaluation environments or characterize Astra’s pretraining exposure. Astra’s access to task-specific demonstrations is defined separately by the ICL and zero-shot conditions.
analysis: We systematically evaluate GPT-6-Astra High as an embodied policy, contrasting its characteristics with prevailing Vision-Action baselines. Astra demonstrates notable performance under direct EEF control, exceeding the average level of existing policies. In what follows, we report its overall performance on EBench and conduct an itemized breakdown of its advantages and drawbacks, providing an overarching evaluation of agentic control in robotic manipulation.
overall: Table 1 compares Astra with seven VLA/WAM policies on EBench. Astra achieves a total SR of 46.73% and Score of 0.6537, ranking second on both measures among the eight systems in this comparison. OpenWAM-α leads with 55.32% SR and 0.7005 Score, leaving gaps of 8.59 percentage points (pp) and 0.0468, respectively. Astra exceeds the remaining six submissions on both metrics, including Qwen-RobotManip and π₀.₅.

This performance is obtained under the one-demonstration in-context learning (ICL) condition: each task is accompanied by 10–18 annotated reference images and their associated guidance, without task-specific parameter updates during evaluation. The result shows that a general-purpose multimodal model can be competitive with specialized robot policies when given compact task-specific context. The following analysis examines where that competitiveness is strongest and what prevents Astra from matching the best overall submission. The main cohort contains only the ICL condition, so its performance does not by itself quantify the gain attributable to demonstrations.

We adopt ICL prompting over zero-shot execution based on an independent exploratory study, detailed in Section 4. Given that EBench tasks are derived from diverse real-world scenarios with ambiguous initial instructions, in-context demonstrations provide essential guidance, enabling Astra to leverage human prior experience rather than engaging in unconstrained, trial-and-error exploration. To substantiate this rationale, supplementary experiments are reported in Appendix ??; notably, these exploratory trials are strictly isolated from the primary 510-episode benchmark cohort.
mobile: Astra achieves 56.58% SR and a 0.7300 Score across the 19 mobile tasks, ranking second only to OpenWAM-α. Notably, its mobile SR trails OpenWAM-α(60.18%) by merely 3.60 pp, whereas its absolute SR drops to 20.00% on fixed-base tasks. This contrast underscores Astra’s competitive edge when manipulation is coupled with mobility, demanding robust spatial reasoning and viewpoint adjustments within a larger workspace.

Task-level evaluations further elucidate Astra’s behavioral advantages over state-of-the-art VLA and WAM policies. Specifically, Astra achieves a 100% SR across all 20 episodes of remote_to_holder (vs. 65% for OpenWAM-α), and 95% on soap_to_dish (vs. 85% for OpenWAM-α and 100% for π₀.₅). While not uniformly dominant across all mobile scenarios, these results highlight Astra’s strong proficiency in mobile manipulation. A plausible interpretation is that Astra’s general multimodal priors effectively map object-centric goals to coordinated base and arm kinematics. Although strict ablation of these priors from active exploration remains for future work, Astra’s performance suggests a capacity for spatial generalization rather than mere trajectory memorization.
clutter: In the bookmark_on_book task, Astra attains a 90% SR, significantly outperforming the closest baseline, π₀.₅ (55%), and the remaining six submissions (ranging from 25% to 45%). Successfully executing this task heavily relies on precise target disambiguation and manipulation within a cluttered environment. Consequently, this substantial 35 pp margin provides strong end-to-end evidence for Astra’s superior visual grounding capabilities, even without decoupled metrics for pure recognition or localization. Figure 1 visualizes successful rollouts for both bookmark and remote manipulation tasks.
perturbations: Across EBench’s object, background, instruction, and mixed perturbations, Astra obtains 44.17%, 50.77%, 44.62%, and 46.15% SR, respectively (Table 2). It ranks second on object variation, third on background variation, fourth on instruction variation, and first on mixed variation in this comparison. The mixed result exceeds OpenWAM-α by only two successes out of 130 episodes, so this ordering should not be interpreted as a reliable advantage. Restricting every category to the common 24 tasks preserves these relative positions.

The perturbation results extend the task-specific examples to a broader set of changed objects, scenes, and instructions. They indicate useful task-conditioned robustness, while the remaining failures show that generalization is not solved. The same reference demonstration is retained across each task’s variations; this comparison does not test transfer to unseen task definitions. Perturbation groups are matched by task and seed, assuming the same category assignment across evaluation versions.
precision: The strongest limitation is the transition from coarse manipulation to precise contact. Astra’s SR falls from 60.60% on low-precision tasks to 40.21% on medium-precision tasks and 11.25% on high-precision tasks (Table 1). The low-to-high difference is 49.35 pp; high-precision SR is approximately 18.6% of low-precision SR. Its position changes from second to third to seventh across these groups. Every compared system performs worse on the high-precision subset than on the low-precision subset, but Astra’s relative standing deteriorates especially sharply (Figure 2).

The assembly tasks make this limitation concrete: Astra achieves only 15% SR on install_gear, 20% on peg_in_hole, and 10% on tighten_nut. Yet their Scores are 0.2000, 0.6000, and 0.5500, respectively. In particular, the separation between Score and SR on peg insertion and nut tightening is consistent with substantial partial progress that does not reliably become completed assembly. The selected peg episode in Figure 3 illustrates this distinction without assigning a unique cause to the failure.

Uncertainty about surface height, object-relative clearance, and contact geometry is a plausible contributor. RGB observations and robot-frame end-effector positions do not directly specify these quantities. Reaching the neighborhood of a target can therefore be easier than aligning and maintaining the contact needed to complete it. This interpretation preserves the distinction between successful object transport and precise assembly; it does not establish a measured advantage in planar localization over depth estimation.
horizon: Astra’s second major limitation is maintaining progress through a complete task. Its SR falls from 53.60% on short-horizon tasks to 28.10% on long-horizon tasks, changing from second to fifth among the compared systems. OpenWAM-α retains 51.43% SR on the long-horizon subset. Astra nevertheless has the highest short-horizon Score (0.6737), narrowly above OpenWAM-α(0.6687), whereas its long-horizon Score is 0.5994 against OpenWAM-α’s 0.7872. The deficit thus remains visible in both complete success and partial-credit performance.

Individual tasks reinforce this pattern. On detergent, Astra reaches 55% SR and 0.8000 Score, compared with OpenWAM-α’s 95% SR. On dishwasher, Astra’s 0.5333 Score accompanies only 5% SR, compared with 90% SR for OpenWAM-α. The selected bottle episode shows another form of incomplete execution: some bottles reach the tray, but several remain outside it at the end (Figure 3). Bottle and shop have zero SR for every compared system, so they illustrate shared difficulty rather than explain Astra’s relative SR gap.

The observed tendency to revisit unsuccessful approaches can help recover a local action, but also consume the resources needed for later stages. Here the policy sees the elapsed timestep without an explicit numeric remaining-step budget; the finite backend limit still applies. Moreover, executing a batch of waypoints delays the next model observation until the batch returns. Together, these conditions motivate examining how retries, feedback timing, and stage planning interact. They do not show that more time alone would resolve the deficit. The practical challenge is to repair a local error while preserving already achieved goals and completing the remaining sequence.
behaviorIntroduction: Qualitative observations help interpret this benchmark profile. Access to two arms does not automatically produce coordinated manipulation: one arm may need to preserve a grasp while the other changes the surrounding geometry. This makes relative poses and contact states important planning variables. Likewise, large translational or rotational corrections raise a safety question beyond simulated task completion; executable simulator motions still require assessment of speed, acceleration, contact forces, and collision risk before hardware deployment. Neither bimanual coordination nor hardware safety is directly measured by the aggregate SR tables.
coffee: On collect_coffee_beans, Astra has no complete successes despite a mean Score of 0.2357. The saved prompt and action descriptions make the distinction between a supplied strategy and its execution concrete:

Later requests describe adjusting the height and tilt of a finger-based scraping motion. The episode ends with Score 0.5 and no complete success. These records show attempts to correct contact geometry, but do not establish that the robot measured the table height or achieved the intended contact. The prompt itself provides both a correction rule and the demonstration’s division of labor between the hands (Appendix ??).
utensils: The low 10% SR on utensils_to_holder also motivates examining how reference guidance is interpreted. In episode 000, the task requests placement “into the utensil holder”, while the annotation admits a less clear terminal arrangement:

The episode ends with Score 0.5 and SR 0. The quoted action supports a compartment-directed interpretation, but the supplied text also encourages that interpretation. It therefore cannot establish that Astra rejected an explicit tray-placement instruction. Later requests describe fork recovery and tray readjustment, leaving several possible contributors to incomplete execution (Appendix ??).
fruit: A related tension appears when the live instruction and the historical example name different destinations:

This episode receives Score 0.6 and SR 0. The ICL explicitly defers the required final container to the live instruction, so the selected action is not evidence of simple refusal to follow guidance. Instead, it illustrates the need to reconcile task wording with demonstrated object roles. Determining whether the container choice caused failure requires evidence beyond the quoted intention and terminal score (Appendix ??).
behaviorClosing: The positive counterpart is Astra’s willingness to revise its actions. Recorded histories contain repeated approaches, gripper closures, and readjustments after unsuccessful attempts. Qualitative observations also suggest that it can articulate an explanation of a failed action and use it to guide another attempt within the episode. Together with its mobile-task performance, these behaviors motivate studying recovery, active exploration, and the retention of useful experience. The central question is how to turn local correction into reliable task completion. Such feedback-driven revision is relevant to future embodied self-improvement, including RSI; the present results demonstrate neither recursive improvement across episodes nor a measured recovery advantage over the comparison policies.
iclIntroduction: To understand how in-context learning (ICL) affects Astra’s embodied behavior, we compare zero-shot and demonstration-conditioned rollouts on Frame Against Pen Holder and Install Gear, as shown in Fig.4.
iclFrame: In the photo-frame task, zero-shot execution demonstrates reaching and moving the target, repeatedly adjusts its approach and wrist orientation without completing the required manipulation. After observing a demonstration, Astra adopts a more appropriate grasp orientation and coordinates both grippers to manipulate the frame, then positions the frame over the cup.
iclGear: In the gear installation task, zero-shot execution likewise demonstrates basic object-handling ability: Astra grasps and lifts the gear, but its placement attempts leave the gear outside the intended assembly position, and installation remains incomplete. With ICL, it positions the gear in the gap between the two existing gears, lowers it into place, releases it, and withdraws the gripper, leaving the gear installed.
iclSummary: Together, these cases suggest that in-context learning can supply task-specific geometric and procedural cues that help translate high-level task intent into executable interaction strategies. Their value lies not merely in clarifying what to manipulate, but in guiding how to grasp, bimanual coordinate, and place objects precisely to satisfy the task objective.
comparisonIntroduction: To examine how general-purpose embodied reasoning differs from task-specialized policy execution, we compare selected rollouts of GPT-6-Astra, π₀.₅, and OpenWAM on Teacup to Saucer and Put Glass in Glassbox, as shown in Fig.5.
recovery: In the teacup task, GPT-6-Astra initially targets the handle region and adjusts its wrist and gripper configuration across successive attempts before securing the teacup and teapot. This behavior is consistent with affordance-informed grasp selection and replanning. After initially placing the cup on the saucer, subsequent manipulation displaces it. GPT-6-Astra later revisits the cup, re-establishes a grasp, and carries it back toward the saucer, demonstrating a response to an invalidated state rather than simply continuing the preceding action sequence. In contrast, π₀.₅ performs repeated approach and retraction motions without completing the cup transfer. OpenWAM attempts to grasp the cup but failed, then moves the teapot onto the tray while leaving the cup off the saucer. The contrast therefore concerns not only object-handling ability, but whether ongoing execution is redirected to resolve unmet or disrupted task requirements.
fine: The glasses packing task exposes a different limitation. GPT-6-Astra successfully performs the coarse bimanual transfer, while the breakdown occurs during the subsequent adjustments needed to fold the temples and close the lid. The temples remain protruding after manipulation, obstructing closure, and further corrective contacts do not resolve the packing problem. This rollout indicates the distinction between making planning toward a task goal and satisfying its final requirements: GPT-6-Astra completes the initial placement but struggles with the precise folding and alignment needed for closure. In the π₀.₅ rollout, the glasses are placed in the case and the temples are folded into a more compact state, although the lid remains open at the end. OpenWAM additionally completes lid closure after the folding sequence. These results highlight more accurate execution of the fine-grained manipulation by the specialized policies.
comparisonSummary: Together, the two tasks reveal complementary capability: GPT-6-Astra exhibits affordance-directed grasp selection, iterative adjustment, and recovery behavior, whereas the specialized policies execute the precision-sensitive task more accurately. Broad task understanding and observation-conditioned revision do not by themselves guarantee precise physical execution; conversely, successful execution of a familiar action trajectory does not necessarily entail recovery when a task requirement remains unmet.
